blindSummary:
This country is a very safe destination for transgender visitors. Legal gender and name change by self-declaration has been available since 2018, anti-discrimination law covers gender identity and expression across employment, housing and services, hate crime and hate speech are both criminalised for gender identity, and transphobia is a separately tracked hate-crime motive. It also passed the region's first femicide law (2023), with protections for gender minorities.

The framework is politically stable with no rollback movement — a contrast with several neighbouring countries. The main caveat is a documented rise in anti-LGBTQ violence and intimidation: the equality body reported in 2025 that gay men and transgender people are increasingly targeted, and a public-broadcaster investigation documented dating-app ambush attacks on queer men in urban nightlife.

For a visitor this is a safe environment with the usual urban-nightlife caution: zero legal exposure, functioning institutions, and a welcoming day-to-day climate, particularly in the capital.
blindOutOfScope: No trans-specific travel advisory; ordinary urban crime in the capital affects all tourists.
blindSourceSummaries: International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): this country has robust protections - discrimination, hate crimes and hate speech on grounds of SOGIESC banned; same-sex marriage and adoption; legal name and gender-marker change based on self-determination; the region's first femicide law (2023) covers all gender-based homicide; a 2023 law bans conversion practices; medically unnecessary surgeries on intersex infants remain legal, though a capital court held a hospital accountable for nonconsensual interventions.

A country page on a regional LGBTI legal-equality index: this country's overall score and per-category compliance breakdown (legal gender recognition, hate crime, equality & non-discrimination, family, civil society, asylum, intersex).

Public broadcaster (May 2025): despite this country's progressive reputation, equality bodies report rising violence and intimidation targeting LGBTQI people, with gay men and trans people especially affected. Of 136 sexual-orientation discrimination cases handled by the equality body in a year, 35% involved physical assault and 35% serious intimidation. A recurring pattern is 'dating app traps' - gay men lured via apps, ambushed, beaten and robbed; a high-profile case against three men accused of targeting at least eight victims went to a capital criminal court in May 2025.

Queer-culture magazine (Feb 2025) summarising a public-broadcaster investigation into rising homophobic attacks in this country orchestrated through dating apps: perpetrators use fake profiles to arrange meetings, then ambush victims in isolated locations where they are robbed, humiliated or assaulted; police have recorded an alarming number of incidents, many unreported due to fear or shame.

Regional security-organisation page on this country's hate-crime frameworks: hate crimes are not defined in legislation and no code exists to record them as such; violations of non-discrimination law that constitute criminal offences are prosecuted under general provisions instead.

Official capital-region page on changing gender registration on ID cards: free of charge, 3-6 weeks processing, requires a valid identity document, a medical certificate attesting to sex change, and possibly a judicial or administrative decision; application made in person at the municipality, digital mode available.

Federal justice department page: since 1 January 2018 (under a law passed mid-2017), trans people can change registered gender and first names without medical conditions, via a declaration to the civil registrar. In June 2019 the constitutional court partially annulled the law; pending new provisions, applications continue under the current procedure.

A travel company's country guide: this country is described as among the safest and most welcoming destinations for LGBTQIA+ travellers worldwide, with forward-thinking attitudes and a thriving queer culture in its major cities.

Country guide (2024): overview of LGBT+ rights history and current status - sex between men decriminalised as far back as 1795 under a modernising civil code of that era, though public-indecency laws and police harassment persisted; covers key figures, organisations, current rights, and where to report homophobia.

'Being transgender - ten years later' (2017), a survey study for the national equality institute: large survey of trans people in this country covering gender identity, coming out, openness, obstacles to living according to one's gender identity, being addressed per experienced gender, official name/gender registration change, work, sex work, economic status and well-being.

Press release (May 2017) from the justice minister on the country's new transgender law: self-determination is the starting point - legal gender change via a purely administrative procedure with all medical conditions (including sterilisation/surgery) scrapped; includes a reflection period and public-order safeguards; notes name-change requests rose from 85 (2012) to 187 (2016).
blindLocalsOnly: The self-declaration legal-gender-recognition process (since 2018, with the constitutional reform that removed the former forced-divorce requirement) is a resident-facing administrative procedure.
blindTangential: Dating-app ambush attacks on queer men documented in urban nightlife — a caution for trans visitors using apps.
